posts.title: What documents you need to rent a self-drive car in Tamil Nadu
posts.metaTitle: Documents Needed to Rent a Self Drive Car in Tamil Nadu
posts.description: The licence, ID and deposit you need to take a self-drive car in Tamil Nadu, what changes for visitors from abroad, and what is checked at handover.
posts.excerpt: A driving licence, one photo ID and a refundable deposit is the short answer. The longer answer covers international permits, what a learner's licence will not do, and what actually gets checked when the car arrives.

body.v: This is the question we are asked most often, and the short answer is dull: an original driving licence, one photo ID, and a refundable deposit. It is the exceptions that cost people a morning, so they are worth setting out properly.
The licence

It has to be an original, valid, and for the class of vehicle you are taking — a car licence for a car, a two-wheeler licence for a scooter. A photograph of it on your phone is not enough, and neither is a photocopy. We take a copy at handover and give the original straight back to you; nobody should be asking to keep your licence for the length of the rental.

A learner's licence will not do. It is not a matter of policy on our side: a learner's licence requires a qualified driver in the passenger seat, which is the opposite of what self-drive means, and the insurance on the vehicle is written on that basis.
One photo ID besides the licence

Aadhaar, a passport, a voter ID or a PAN card all work. The point of the second document is simply that it is issued by somebody other than the transport department, so the two together are harder to fake than either alone.
If you are visiting from abroad

Bring your home licence, your passport, and an international driving permit alongside the home licence — the permit is a translation, not a licence in itself, so it is only valid presented with the original. If you hold an Indian licence and live overseas, that is simpler: the Indian licence alone is fine.
Visitors home for a few weeks usually want an automatic, and there is normally one of those rather than six, so it is worth asking for it before you land rather than on the morning you want it.
The deposit

A refundable security deposit is standard across the industry and it is not a fee. It is held while you have the vehicle and returned when the vehicle comes back, less anything owing for kilometres beyond the agreed allowance or for damage. The figure depends on the vehicle, and you should be told it before you book rather than when you arrive to collect.
What actually gets checked at handover

v: The odometer reading, written down in front of you
The fuel level, noted the same way
Existing marks on the bodywork, walked round together
The date and time the vehicle is due back

body.v: Five minutes of this at the start is what stops a disagreement at the end. If a rental does not do it, ask them to — and if they will not, that tells you something.
The one thing people forget

Kilometre limits. Every self-drive rental includes a daily allowance, and anything past it is charged per kilometre. Both numbers should be on your booking before you leave. A day trip to Kanyakumari and back from Nagercoil is about forty kilometres; a day that takes in Padmanabhapuram and the falls at Thirparappu can be a hundred and fifty. Those are very different against a limit, and it is better to know which you are planning.

posts.title: A one-day Kanyakumari drive, with honest timings
posts.metaTitle: One Day in Kanyakumari by Self Drive Car — Itinerary
posts.description: A Kanyakumari day by car that actually fits: the point, Vattakottai, Suchindram and Padmanabhapuram, with real driving times and closing hours.
posts.excerpt: Most one-day Kanyakumari itineraries are written by people who have not driven them. This one has the distances, the closing times and the bit where the ferry queue eats an hour.

body.v: The sights around Kanyakumari are close together, which makes a one-day plan look easier on a map than it is. The distances are short; the queues, the temple hours and the parking are what fill the day. Here is a route that fits, with the timings that make it fit.
Before sunrise — leave Nagercoil by 5:15

It is about twenty kilometres from Nagercoil to Kanyakumari, and at that hour it takes half an hour. Leaving at a quarter past five gets you parked and walking with time to spare. If you are staying in Kanyakumari itself, ten minutes is enough, which is the main argument for staying the night.
The point, and the ferry

Sunrise from the shore is free and takes as long as you want. The ferry to the Vivekananda Rock is the decision: in season the queue can be an hour each way, and that is the single thing most likely to break the rest of the day. If you want the Rock, do it first and accept that the afternoon will be shorter. If you would rather see more, skip it and come back another morning.
Vattakottai — 6 km up the coast

Fifteen minutes' drive north along the coast road, and one of the better short drives in the district with the sea on your right the whole way. The fort itself needs half an hour. It is quieter early, and the wind picks up as the morning goes on.
Suchindram — 13 km inland

The Thanumalayan temple, about twenty-five minutes from Vattakottai. The important thing here is the timing: like most temples in the district it closes in the middle of the day and opens again in the late afternoon. Aim to arrive before noon or plan to come back at four — driving there at one o'clock means looking at a closed gate.
Padmanabhapuram Palace — 35 km on

The wooden palace at Thuckalay, roughly an hour from Suchindram allowing for traffic through Nagercoil. It closes earlier than people expect and it does not admit anyone in the last part of the afternoon, so this is the stop to check the hours for on the day rather than to assume. An hour and a half inside is about right; it is bigger than it looks.
What the day adds up to

v: About 80 to 90 km of driving in total
Roughly three hours behind the wheel, spread across the day
The rest is walking, queuing and looking at things
Sunset back at Kanyakumari if you have the energy; most people do not

body.v: Doing it yourself, or with a driver

Self-drive suits this day if you like setting your own pace and you do not mind parking. Every stop involves leaving the car somewhere crowded and walking back to it afterwards, which is the honest argument for taking a driver instead — the driving is the easy part and the parking is not. Either works; it depends which of those bothers you more.

posts.title: Self drive or with a driver? An honest comparison
posts.metaTitle: Self Drive or With a Driver in Kanyakumari District?
posts.description: When self drive is the better choice in Kanyakumari district and when a driver earns their rate — parking, temple timings, night runs and long highway days.
posts.excerpt: We rent vehicles both ways, so we have no stake in the answer. Here is when each one is genuinely the better choice, including the days when self drive is a false economy.

body.v: We rent vehicles with a driver and without one, so there is no answer here that suits us better than the other. There is a real difference between the two, though, and it is not mainly about money.
Take self drive when

v: You are staying put and making short trips — errands, the market, visiting family across town
You want to leave when you feel like it, including before dawn and after dinner
You are comfortable in Indian traffic, or you are taking an automatic and the roads are quiet
The trip is flexible and you would rather decide as you go

body.v: Self drive is also usually cheaper for a day of ordinary running around, because you are paying for the vehicle and not for somebody's time. If your day is two short trips and a lot of sitting still, a driver spends most of it waiting, and you pay for the waiting.
Take a driver when

v: The day is a sightseeing circuit with a stop every half hour — the parking, not the driving, is the work
You are going a long way on the highway, particularly to Thiruvananthapuram or Madurai
There is an airport run at an unsociable hour
It is a wedding, or any day where the family should not be driving
Nobody in the group knows the roads and the timings

body.v: The thing people underestimate

Temple and monument hours. Most of the places worth visiting in this district shut in the middle of the day and open again late afternoon, and they are not all the same hours. A driver who does this every week knows which one to go to first; somebody with a map finds out by driving to a closed gate. Over a full day that is an hour or two, and it is the difference between seeing four things and seeing two.
The false economy

A long highway day self-driven, by somebody who is tired and does not know the road. The saving is real and it is not worth it. If the day involves three hours each way and an early start, take the driver and sleep in the back on the way home.
You can mix them

Nothing stops you renting self drive for a week in town and taking a vehicle with a driver for the one day you are doing the circuit. That is what a lot of families visiting for a fortnight end up doing, and it is usually the cheapest version of a good trip rather than a compromise.

posts.title: KM limits, extra-KM rates and deposits, explained plainly
posts.metaTitle: Self Drive Car KM Limits and Deposits — Nagercoil
posts.description: What a daily kilometre limit means, how extra-KM charges add up, and what a refundable deposit really covers. The three numbers to agree before you drive.
posts.excerpt: Three numbers decide what a self-drive rental actually costs, and only one of them is the daily rate. Here is what the other two mean and how to work out whether a quote is a good one.

body.v: A daily rate on its own does not tell you what a rental costs. Three numbers do, and the other two are the ones that turn a cheap-looking quote into an expensive week.
1. The daily rate

What the vehicle costs for a day. It should come down for a longer rental — a week priced at seven times a day is not a weekly rate, it is a daily rate repeated. Ask for the weekly and monthly figures even if you are only thinking about a weekend, because a business that has them has thought about this properly.
2. The kilometre allowance

How far you can drive each day before extra charges start. This is where quotes differ most and where people get caught. A generous daily rate with a small allowance is often worse than the reverse, and which is better depends entirely on your trip.

Some real distances from Nagercoil, one way: Kanyakumari is 20 km, Suchindram 7, Thuckalay 18, Marthandam 30, Colachel 30, Thiruvananthapuram about 65. A day pottering around town might be 40 km. A day that takes in the palace, the falls and the point can be 150. Against a 150 km allowance those are very different days.
3. The extra-kilometre rate

What each kilometre past the allowance costs. It is usually a single-figure rupee amount, which sounds like nothing until you are sixty kilometres over on each of five days. Work it out against your actual plan rather than against the rate, and if you know you will go over, say so at the start — it is normally cheaper to agree a bigger allowance up front than to pay the overage.
What a deposit actually covers

A refundable security deposit is not a fee and it is not a part-payment. It is held while you have the vehicle, and it comes back when the vehicle does, minus anything genuinely owing: kilometres past the allowance, fuel if you return it lower than you took it, and damage. Nothing else should come out of it.
Questions worth asking anyone, including us

v: What is the daily allowance, and what does a kilometre past it cost?
What is the deposit, and when exactly does it come back?
Is the fuel level recorded at handover, in writing?
What happens if I keep the vehicle a day longer than planned?
Who pays if it breaks down?

body.v: A rental that answers all five without hesitating is one you can plan around. One that answers in round numbers and changes the subject is one to keep looking past.

posts.title: Driving in Kanyakumari district: roads, monsoon and what to expect
posts.metaTitle: Self Drive in Kanyakumari District — Roads and Monsoon
posts.description: What the roads are really like across Kanyakumari district, how the monsoon changes them, and the local habits worth knowing before you drive here.
posts.excerpt: The highways are good, the town centres are slow, and the inland roads have more going on than the map suggests. What to expect, season by season.

body.v: Kanyakumari district is small and varied. You can go from a fast four-lane highway to a street laid out before cars existed in about ten minutes, and the driving on each is a different job.
The main roads

The highway between Nagercoil, Kanyakumari and on towards Thiruvananthapuram is in good condition and moves well. The coast road from Kanyakumari up towards Vattakottai and Colachel is tarred, scenic and genuinely windy — there is nothing between it and the sea, and that tells on a tall vehicle or a two-wheeler most afternoons.
The town centres

Nagercoil's centre is heavy for most of the day, and the streets around the Nagaraja temple and the market were not built for cars. If you are passing through rather than stopping, take the bypass; if you are stopping, park before ten in the morning or expect to walk. The same is true in a smaller way of Suchindram and Thuckalay around the temples.
Inland, and the hills

Going inland towards Thiruvattar, Thirparappu and the hills the surface gets patchier and the corners tighten. Nothing there needs a four-wheel drive or high clearance, but it does reward a softer-riding car and an unhurried pace. Watch for buses on the narrow sections — they will take their half out of the middle and they are not going to be the ones to give way.
The monsoon

This district gets rain from both monsoons, and the heavier one is the north-east, roughly October to December. What changes is not so much the road as the visibility and the standing water: the low stretches flood briefly and drain quickly, and the sensible response is to wait twenty minutes rather than to drive into water you cannot see the bottom of. Rain also brings the two-wheelers closer together at junctions, so leave more room than usual.
Local habits worth knowing

v: A horn here means 'I am here', not 'get out of the way' — use it on blind corners
Overtaking happens on both sides; check your mirrors before moving out
Buses and lorries assume right of way on narrow roads, and it is easier to let them have it
Livestock on inland roads is normal, and it does not look before crossing
After dark on unlit stretches, expect unlit vehicles too

body.v: If you have not driven in India before

Take an automatic, start in the morning rather than the evening, and give yourself the first day on quieter roads before taking on Nagercoil at five in the afternoon. It settles down faster than people expect — the traffic looks chaotic and is mostly predictable, and once you stop being surprised by it you are fine.
